subject: Banking
title: Remittances and the Migrant Tax
description: A quick win: understand Remittances and the Migrant Tax.

hook.text: Migrant workers sent $656 billion home in 2022. The average fee to send $200 is 6.2%.

buildup.text: Remittances are the largest financial flow to developing nations. For many families, they are the primary income source.

discovery.text: Fees are high because transfers cross multiple currencies, banks, and regulatory jurisdictions. Each step adds cost.

twist.text: Mobile money services like M-Pesa cut fees to 3% or less.

climax.text: Remittance fees are a tax on the world's poorest workers. Lowering them by 5% would save $32 billion annually.

punchline.text: $40 billion in fees on family money. The poorest pay the most.

quiz.question: Why are remittance fees so high?
options: Transfers cross multiple currencies, banks, and regulatory jurisdictions

details.summary: Migrant workers send over 600 billion dollars home annually in remittances, but traditional transfer services charge an average of 6 percent in fees, effectively taxing some of the world's poorest families.
details.whyItMatters: Remittances exceed foreign aid to developing countries by a factor of three. Reducing transfer costs by just a few percentage points would put billions more into the hands of families that need it most.
takeaways: Global remittances exceed 600 billion dollars annually
Average transfer fees remain around 6 percent of the amount sent
Digital services like Wise and Remitly are reducing costs significantly

faq.question: Why are remittance fees so high?
faq.answer: Legacy providers like Western Union maintain expensive agent networks. Compliance costs for anti-money-laundering regulations are substantial. Limited competition in many corridors allows providers to maintain high margins.

faq.question: Can cryptocurrency reduce remittance costs?
faq.answer: In theory, yes. Some corridors use stablecoins to bypass expensive correspondent banking chains. In practice, converting between crypto and local currency adds costs, and recipients in developing countries often need cash.
